newsitem.title: FRANCE: Saint Laurent opens Paris shows, defends his turf.
newsitem.headline: Saint Laurent opens Paris shows, defends his turf.

text.p: Yves Saint-Laurent kicked off the autumn-winter ready-to-wear season on Monday as Paris struggled to save its reputation as the world's fashion capital after the critical hits of the London and Milan collections.

For the second consecutive season, France's living fashion legend shunned the crowds and crush of the catwalk and presented a sample 31 outfits to a tiny audience of some 20 reporters and photographers in his plush couture salon.
"We are doing this to create an aspect of friendly proximity," said Saint-Laurent's feisty president Pierre Berge.
Flamboyant swan feather coats, flashy three-tone jersey dresses, and a gold lame dinner tunic aside, Saint-Laurent's razor-edged tailoring and cool elegance took on a minimalist flavour.
It showed in the starkness of a sleeveless black satin slipdress, austere black coats on skinny trousers or transparent tee-shirts and slacks of stretchy onion-skin jersey.
Carla Bruni was pert and childlike in velvet kneepants and a matching beret, Sybil Buck statuesque in a splashy red maxi coat and Karen Mulder slender and sexy in a jumpsuit of sequin swirls.

Questioned after the show, Berge shrugged off suggestions that Paris was loosing its grip as the epicentre of fashion as British upstarts grab the headlines and business-minded Italians and Americans outsell their French rivals.

"People are confusing creation and marketing. The kings of marketing are in Milan, with Gucci and Prada, or in New York, with Calvin Klein and Donna Karan. But the creativity is still in France," he said.

To prove Saint Laurent's superiority over the likes of Britain's John Galliano, whose debut collection for former Saint Laurent employer Christian Dior was the triumph of January's couture shows, Berge said Saint Laurent had tripled his haute couture sales in the year to January 1997.

Last month, Saint Laurent created a stir when he told the German magazine Focus that the couture collections by Galliano and fellow Briton Alexander McQueen, the new designer for Givenchy, were "ridiculous spectacles which would have been more in keeping with a rock concert. I was totally bored with their shows."
McQueen savaged critics in the French fashion press in an interview to appear in the weekly magazine Newsweek, bizzarely comparing them to Hitler.

"My clothes are out there on a limb and I get slagged for it. It's like Hitler and the Holocaust. He destroyed millions of people because he didn't understand. That's what a lot of people have done to me because they can't understand what I do," he said.
